text.p: A senior Belarussian official dismissed a claim by a previously unheard-of group opposed to union with Russia that it was reponsible for a blast that shut down a gas pipeline this week, Interfax-West news agency said on Friday.

The agency quoted an alleged statement from the Belarussian Liberation Army saying the pipeline blast and an accident at a gas plant in Minsk region last month were "a warning to integrators in Moscow and their Belarussian lackeys".
But Interfax later quoted an unnamed senior security official as dismissing the notion of a guerrilla attack, saying political forces were taking advantage of "coincidence".
Experts at the stricken pipeline tended to think that the blast was due to the age of the pipes, laid in 1975, he said.
A press spokesman for the KGB security service told Reuters he had no information such a claim had been made.

A Beltransgaz official said she could not confirm that anyone had claimed responsibility for the blast which shut down the pipeline taking supplies from Russia to Poland about 60 km (40 miles) south of the capital Minsk on April 30.

An Interfax reporter told Reuters that the statement had been delivered to the newspaper Svaboda (Freedom), which opposes Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko and the union treaty he signed with Russia last month.

Nationalists are bitterly opposed to Lukashenko's plans to unite with neighbouring Russia, fearing it could mean a return to the domination from Moscow they thought they threw off when the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991.
Lukashenko signed the Union Treaty with Russian President Boris Yeltsin on April 2 and talks are going on about how it will be implemented and how close ties will be.
